title.narrative: 2022-25 Bangladesh Rohingya and Host Communities Humanitarian Package

description.narrative: The Rohingya crisis is the largest and most complex humanitarian crisis in the Indo-Pacific region. As per the 2023 Response Plan (JRP) 1.52 million people need humanitarian assistance in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, including both Rohingya refugees and impacted host communities. The Bangladesh Rohingya and Host Community Humanitarian Package (2022-2025) is the country level humanitarian response to this cross border crisis originating in Myanmar and causing large-scale displacement into Bangladesh. The Bangladesh package objective is to contribute to international efforts to meet humanitarian and protection needs and increase self-reliance and resilience of Rohingya and host populations in Bangladesh. The aim is to meet refugees and host communities’ basic needs; increase their self-reliance; build resilience and social cohesion; and improve the effectiveness of the humanitarian system. The total estimated investment value is $190m over 3 years, starting in 2022-23.

description.narrative: : In 2024, Australia’s humanitarian assistance played a key role in strengthening disease preparedness in the Rohingya refugee camps, with a strong focus on training and capacity building through the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Given the high risk of communicable disease outbreaks in the overcrowded camps, Australia supported two IOM-operated Infectious Disease Treatment Centres and several primary healthcare facilities. These centres treated 7,798 dengue outpatients and 817 inpatients with moderate-to-severe cases. IOM also managed 52 suspected diphtheria cases and treated 8,588 outpatients and 224 inpatients with acute watery diarrhea. In addition to clinical care, IOM prioritized building local health capacity. A total of 63 healthcare workers and 215 community health workers (CHWs) were trained in sexual and reproductive health (SRH), disease management, and emergency response. These efforts enhanced frontline readiness for early detection, treatment, and containment of outbreaks. IOM provided ongoing supervision and skills development to ensure healthcare providers could respond effectively to evolving health threats. This integrated approach combined service delivery with workforce development to strengthen the resilience of health systems in one of the world’s most vulnerable communities.

Australia supports the BRAC Localisation Pooled Fund in the Rohingya response to strengthen locally led humanitarian action. Through this initiative, 27 Bangladeshi NGOs received capacity building across 17 thematic areas, including financial management, safeguarding, monitoring and evaluation, procurement, and human resources. These efforts led to tangible improvements in accountability, transparency, and operational efficiency. Notably, 10 NGOs reported stronger HR systems, improved recruitment processes, and enhanced safeguarding protocols. Several NGOs that BRAC supported have since secured additional donor funding, expanded their programming, and taken on leadership roles in sector coordination platforms, particularly in WASH and education. ‍ Australia also supports inclusive governance through UNHCR and the Australia Assists program. In 2024, a Disability Inclusion Officer deployed to UNHCR helped integrate disability-disaggregated data into protection monitoring tools, addressing underreporting of GBV among women with disabilities. This led to the creation of mobile outreach teams for confidential survivor support and strengthened referral pathways. These initiatives reflect Australia’s commitment to inclusive, accountable, and resilient humanitarian governance.

Australia’s funding advanced gender equality by supporting gender-responsive programming and channelling resources and support to women-led organizations in the Rohingya response. BRAC’s Localisation Fund directly provides capacity building support to nine women-led organisations and networks, empowering their ability to deliver services to Rohingya and Host Communities. Australia’s support to UN Women enabled two national women’s rights organizations (ASK and Nari Maitree) to deliver behaviour change programming and community outreach. UN Women leveraged its close partnership with local women’s organisations to facilitate agreement on inclusion of four women’s organisations as standing members of the Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, establishing and strengthening the role of local women-led CSOs as a key source of guidance for the response. UN Women engaged Rohingya-led women’s network to assist them in gender assessments, psychosocial first aid, referrals and awareness-raising activities.

Australia’s humanitarian assistance to Rohingya and Host Communities enabled the delivery of over 86,000 services to survivors of sexual and gender-based violence, including 80 persons with disabilities. Partners such as CARE through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership, BRAC, IOM, and UNICEF provided critical interventions including counselling, health care, legal aid, and safety support. IOM alone delivered over 81,000 services, highlighting the scale and reach of the program. The investment strengthened protection mechanisms for vulnerable populations, particularly women and children, and contributed to building safer, more resilient communities. The integration of SGBV services within broader humanitarian programming ensured survivors received holistic support tailored to their needs.

Australia’s investment in food security in Bangladesh supported over 22,000 individuals through climate-smart agricultural practices. BRAC and UNHCR implemented interventions such as homestead gardening, aquaculture, and livestock rearing. On Bhasan Char, UNHCR’s support led to a 15% increase in crop yields and local self-sufficiency in fish production. BRAC’s training programs restored traditional farming knowledge among Rohingya refugees and enabled income generation through vegetable cultivation and broiler farming. These efforts improved household nutrition and economic stability, demonstrating the value of sustainable agriculture in humanitarian contexts

In 2023, Australian Government partner UNFPA supported health systems strengthening in Bangladesh. Australia supports UNFPA’s midwifery mentorship programme financially and through technical assistance from Australia Assists. International midwife mentors provided onsite and off-site mentorship for 283 national midwives. In 2023, 21 Midwifery Lifesaving Sessions were also conducted by the international midwives, reaching a total of 495 national midwives (note: total results not attributable to DFAT). UNFPA also continues to support referral systems for Rohingya and Host communities through the Matri Sheba – an emergency referral and transport system of 15 ambulances. In 2023, a total of 8,382 mothers were referred to emergency obstetric services

In 2023, Australian funding helped to provide 31, 143 victims-survivors of violence with services such as counselling, referrals, health and legal support. This support was provided through our partners the AHP Care Consortium, UNFPA and UNICEF.

In 2024, Australian humanitarian partners delivering assistance in Rohingya and Host Communities have improved access, strengthened service delivery and institutional capacity of health systems. Humanitarian Partners have reached the population with primary healthcare services such as consultations, information and vaccinations. Australia supported the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) to strengthen referral systems from health facilities in the camps to secondary and tertiary health facilities in the Bangladesh system. IOM and UNFPA operated a fleet of ambulances and shuttle vehicles for routine SRHR access, facilitating 1,964 emergency referrals and supported 1,543 facility-based deliveries by skilled birth attendants. UNFPA trained over 460 health workers, including national midwives and has contributed to a 19% reduction in maternal deaths. These interventions collectively improved the accessibility, quality, and responsiveness of health services in Rohingya and host communities.

In 2024, Australia’s humanitarian assistance in Bangladesh for Rohingya and Host communities supported over 1 million individuals, including over 700,00 women and girls, and 12,400 people with disabilities. Australia’s UN and NGO partners (AHP, BRAC, HI, IOM, UNFPA, UNHCR, UNICEF, UN Women, and WFP) supported the delivery of life-saving food, water and shelter as well as essential protection, education and health services for those most in need, including women, girls and people with disabilities.

Our NGO partners such as BRAC and the Australian Humanitarian Partnerships (AHP) are supporting climate resilient agriculture and improved food security for Rohingya and host communities through livelihood activities. In 2023, Mukti – an implementing partner of CARE in the AHP Consortium provided training in homestead gardening and pit composting, along with material support, to 260 people. This included 225 women and 30 persons with disabilities who through assessments reported a 76% increase in understanding of improved seed and farm management and an 84% increase in understanding of climate-smart agricultural practices. Our support has empowered participants while also contributing to household dietary diversity and addressing food insecurity. (note: results 100% attributable to DFAT).

The Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh is the largest in the world. Australia’s Rohingya and Host Communities Humanitarian Program in Bangladeshis contributing to international efforts to meet humanitarian and protection needs and increase self-reliance and resilience. The program supports the delivery of life-saving food, water and shelter as well as essential protection, education and health services for those most in need, including women, girls and people with disability. In 2023, Australia supported emergency assistance to 864,458 displaced Rohingya people and host communities in Bangladesh, including 43,104 persons living with disability, delivered by the AHP, BRAC (a national NGO), and UN partners.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: Through Australia’s funding, in 2023 our partners were able to help improve 6,125 individuals to better adapt to climate change and/or strengthen their resilience to disasters. This included 129 people with disabilities. In 2023, CARE under the Australian Humanitarian Partnerships worked in coordination with Camp-in-Charge (CiCs) and Site Management Agencies and improved accessibility and mitigated risks for 2,650 people, including 1,527 female and 64 persons with disabilities. This included drainage construction and repairs to direct the flow of stormwater, slope stabilisation to reduce the risk of landslides, and the construction of stairways to improve accessibility for both Rohingya refugees and humanitarian workers. (note: results 100% attributable to DFAT)
